reviewBoundary: Three paired senior readings. Fictional magazines/sign writer/repair day/residency; qualified fruit and draft-analysis discussion. Same-author all-option/evidence review, no invented findings or independent calibration.

units.title: Three magazines and a sign writer
units.alignmentNote: Two complete original passages, three and four four-choice questions, following National I final structure. Old source supplies a level/family reference only.

materials.title: Three magazines for curious readers
materials.text:
The school library is adding three monthly magazines to its reading corner. Students may read the current issue in the library; earlier issues can be borrowed for one week. The descriptions below will help readers choose where to begin.

Field Notes follows everyday wildlife in gardens, streets and small parks. Each issue focuses on observations readers can make without collecting animals or disturbing nests. Short articles explain common patterns, while a regular sketch page shows how to record shape and movement. It suits readers who enjoy looking closely outdoors rather than simply learning lists of species names.

Making It examines ordinary objects from the inside. A recent issue followed a bicycle pump from its handle to its valve. Drawings and interviews explain how materials and moving parts work together. Some issues include simple paper models, but the magazine does not provide instructions for repairing electrical appliances or other hazardous equipment.

Words in Motion is about language in use. It compares signs, conversations, translations and song lyrics, asking how wording changes with purpose and audience. The magazine includes a short fiction section and a column answering readers' questions about expressions they have encountered.

None requires specialist knowledge. Readers who would like a particular older issue should ask at the desk, since earlier copies are kept in storage rather than beside the latest ones. The library welcomes suggestions, but a request does not guarantee that an out-of-print issue can be obtained.

questions.prompt: Which magazine is most suitable for studying a bicycle pump?
options: Field Notes
Words in Motion
Making It
All three focus only on pumps
questions.explanation: Making It explains objects and specifically features a pump. Wildlife/language magazines have other subjects; all-three-only is false.

questions.prompt: What can readers do with a previous issue?
options: Keep it permanently without asking
Demand that every out-of-print copy be supplied
Borrow it for one week if available
Always find it beside the current issue
questions.explanation: Earlier issues are borrowable for a week, stored separately and subject to availability. Permanent keeping/guaranteed supply are not offered.

questions.prompt: What do the magazines have in common?
options: They contain only species lists
They can be read without specialist knowledge
They are published every day
They all teach electrical repairs
questions.explanation: The final paragraph states no specialist knowledge. Hazardous repairs are excluded, subjects differ and all are monthly.

materials.title: The last letter on the shop window
materials.text:
The bakery on our street had a painted name across its window. When it changed owners, the new baker asked a sign writer to add one word beneath it. I watched from outside while waiting for my mother, expecting the work to take only a few minutes.

The sign writer first placed a paper guide inside the window. Then she stepped back and looked from the opposite pavement. A letter that seemed perfectly placed from close up looked crowded at a distance. She moved the guide slightly and checked again.

I asked why she did not measure equal spaces between every letter. She showed me the difference between a narrow letter and a wide one. Equal measured gaps did not always create an even visual rhythm. She was judging how the whole word appeared, not merely the length of each empty strip.

Once satisfied, she began painting. From my side of the glass, her hand seemed to move in an unfamiliar direction. She was working on the inside, arranging the letters so that people outside could read them. It required thinking about the view from the other side.

The final letter took longer than I expected. She adjusted a small curve, then stopped. I could not see what had changed until she pointed to the relationship with its neighbour. The correction was tiny, but the end of the word no longer seemed to lean away.

My mother returned before the paint had dried. On our way home, I noticed other shop signs: hurried printed notices, careful lettering and one partly hidden by a plant. I had expected to watch a person add a word. Instead, I had watched someone design a reading experience from the pavement. The sign's success depended on the position of the person who would use it.

questions.prompt: Why does the sign writer view the guide from across the street?
options: To assess how the letters appear from a reader’s distance
To ask another shop to copy the name
To avoid measuring the glass at all
To let the paper blow away
questions.explanation: The distant view reveals crowding. It does not reject every measurement, request copying or expose paper to wind.

questions.prompt: What does she explain about equal measured gaps?
options: They may not create an even visual effect
They are required only for narrow letters
They remove the need to consider letter shapes
They always make every word unreadable
questions.explanation: Different letter widths affect visual rhythm. The text makes a qualified claim, not universal unreadability or shape irrelevance.

questions.prompt: Why is the direction of painting unfamiliar to the narrator?
options: The narrator is watching through a camera
The sign is painted inside for readers outside
The baker has requested a secret code
The sign writer is deliberately writing nonsense
questions.explanation: Working from inside reverses the painter’s relation to the outside view. Nonsense/camera/code are not stated.

questions.prompt: What is the narrator’s final understanding?
options: Printed notices can never communicate
Every small correction is invisible and useless
Lettering should be judged from the intended reader’s position
A shop name matters only to its painter
questions.explanation: The conclusion centres the pavement reader. Small corrections can help; printed communication is not universally rejected and audience matters.

units.alignmentNote: Two complete original passages, three and four four-choice questions, following National I final structure. Old source supplies a level/family reference only.

materials.title: A repair day with clear limits
materials.text:
The Riverside Community Hall will host a repair day on Sunday from 10:00 to 16:00. Volunteer repairers will examine small household items with visitors. The event aims to share skills and reduce waste, but it is not a commercial repair service and cannot promise a successful repair.

Book a thirty-minute assessment slot and describe your item in advance. Bring one item per booking. Suitable examples include clothing, simple non-electrical toys and small pieces of furniture that one person can carry. Gas appliances, electrical equipment and items involving hazardous materials will not be accepted.

If an instruction booklet or spare part is already available, bring it with the item. Do not dismantle something beyond your knowledge in preparation. A repairer may decide that an item is unsuitable for the session, even if it belongs to a normally accepted category.

Visitors remain with their items and discuss the work with the volunteer. Children under sixteen must attend with an adult. Nobody is expected to use unfamiliar tools without guidance, and volunteers may stop work where they judge conditions unsafe.

The assessment is free. Any proposed material cost will be discussed before it is incurred. If a repair cannot be completed, you must take the item home; the hall is not a waste collection point. Please cancel a booking you no longer need so the slot can be offered to someone else.

questions.prompt: Which item is within the listed scope?
options: A gas heater
A small non-electrical toy
A damaged electrical kettle
A container of hazardous chemicals
questions.explanation: Simple non-electrical toys are included; gas/electrical/hazardous items are excluded.

questions.prompt: What must visitors do during the session?
options: Leave the items and return next month
Use every unfamiliar tool alone
Pay for materials before any discussion
Remain with their items
questions.explanation: Visitors stay and discuss repairs. Tool guidance/cost agreement are required, not abandoned items or automatic prepayment.

questions.prompt: What happens if an item cannot be repaired?
options: The volunteer guarantees a replacement
The visitor takes it home
The booking becomes a permanent storage agreement
The hall automatically disposes of it
questions.explanation: Unrepaired items go home with visitors. Disposal/replacement/storage guarantees are explicitly or implicitly absent.

materials.title: Colour is a clue, not a complete verdict
materials.text:
At a fruit stall, colour is one of the first features a shopper notices. It can provide useful information, but the relationship between colour and readiness to eat is not the same for every fruit or variety. A red surface is not a universal certificate of sweetness.

The visible colour comes from pigments in the fruit's outer tissues. As some fruits develop, changes in pigments can accompany other changes in texture, aroma and flavour. These processes are related, but they are not identical. A fruit may acquire an attractive colour without matching the taste a particular shopper expects.

Variety makes a difference. Two kinds of apple can have different characteristic colours when mature. Comparing a green variety with a red one as though both were following the same colour scale would confuse a difference between varieties with a difference in readiness. The same caution applies to using a photograph of one fruit as a guide to every other.

Growing and storage conditions add further complications. Light exposure may affect the colour on one side, while a shopper sees only the most visible surface. Handling can leave marks that say more about a journey to market than about the fruit's original condition. Neither a perfectly even surface nor a small mark provides a complete account by itself.

This does not mean appearance should be ignored. It means appearance should be interpreted alongside relevant knowledge: which fruit it is, how it normally changes and what the buyer wants to do with it. Fruit intended for cooking may be chosen for different qualities from fruit intended to be eaten immediately.

The stallholder's explanation and the shopper's experience can therefore complement what is visible. Good judgment uses several appropriate clues rather than turning one familiar sign into an automatic rule. Colour remains valuable information, but it becomes more useful when we understand the question it can and cannot answer.

questions.prompt: What is the author’s main caution?
options: Only photographs can show maturity
Colour alone cannot determine every fruit’s eating quality
Fruit appearance should never be considered
All red fruit tastes exactly the same
questions.explanation: The passage argues for interpreted colour among several clues. It rejects universal red sweetness and does not reject appearance.

questions.prompt: Why compare green and red apple varieties?
options: To prove green apples are always immature
To establish that photographs cause pigment changes
To show that different varieties do not share one colour scale
To claim red apples never change
questions.explanation: Characteristic variety colours differ. The other claims are universal or physically unrelated.

questions.prompt: What can a surface mark reveal?
options: A complete history of every stage
The guaranteed amount of sugar
The exact date the fruit will be eaten
Something about handling rather than the original growing condition
questions.explanation: Handling marks may reflect transport. The passage gives no total history, sugar guarantee or eating date.

questions.prompt: What approach does the author recommend?
options: Choose the reddest item for every purpose
Treat all storage conditions as identical
Ignore knowledge from experience
Combine relevant clues according to the fruit and intended use
questions.explanation: Variety, normal changes and use combine with experience. Automatic redness/ignored knowledge/uniform storage contradict the conclusion.

units.alignmentNote: Two complete original passages, three and four four-choice questions, following National I final structure. Old source supplies a level/family reference only.

materials.title: A short residency for essay writers
materials.text:
North Field Arts House invites applications for a two-week essay-writing residency. It is intended for writers with a substantial nonfiction project already under way. Applicants need not have a published book, but they should be able to describe the question and form of the work they plan to develop.

The residency provides a private bedroom, a shared kitchen and a quiet workroom. Travel, meals and personal expenses are not included. There is no requirement to produce a fixed number of pages, and the house does not promise publication or representation.

Submit a project description of no more than 800 words and a sample of between 2000 and 3000 words. Both must be in English. The sample may come from an earlier project if it demonstrates the kind of work relevant to the proposed essay. Do not submit a whole manuscript in place of the requested extract.

Applications close at 17:00 on 30 November. Shortlisted applicants will be invited to a video conversation in December. The selection panel considers the project's clarity, the sample and whether the house's facilities fit the writer's needs; awards or publication history alone do not determine selection.

Residents give one informal discussion about a question arising from their work. This is a conversation with the other residents, not a public performance or a finished-book launch. Access needs should be discussed with the coordinator before accepting a place, since the historic building has limitations that cannot all be removed.

questions.prompt: Who may apply without a published book?
options: A writer with a substantial nonfiction project under way
Anyone seeking guaranteed book publication
Only previous award winners
Only writers submitting an entire manuscript
questions.explanation: The stated eligibility is an existing substantial nonfiction project; book publication and awards are not mandatory or determinative.

questions.prompt: What does the residency include?
options: All travel and meals
Guaranteed representation
A bedroom and shared working/living facilities
A paid public book launch
questions.explanation: Accommodation/kitchen/workroom are included. Travel/meals are excluded and no representation or public launch is promised.

questions.prompt: What is the required resident discussion?
options: An informal exchange about a question from the work
A finished manuscript reading for the public
A substitute for the written application
An awards ceremony deciding selection
questions.explanation: The discussion is with residents about an ongoing question. It is neither public launch, selection ceremony nor application replacement.

materials.title: What an abandoned sentence can show
materials.text:
A writer's draft can be tempting evidence. Crossed-out lines, arrows and replacement words seem to offer a view of thought in motion. Yet the page records marks made during writing, not every thought that led to them. Reading it well requires curiosity and restraint together.

A cancelled sentence shows that a form of words was present and then rejected or displaced. It does not, on its own, establish why. The writer may have changed an argument, avoided repetition, shortened a paragraph or simply moved the sentence elsewhere. A confident account of motive needs more support than a line through the words.

The sequence of revisions can also be uncertain. An arrow may connect two passages without revealing whether they were written minutes or months apart. Different inks or layers of handwriting may suggest an order, but such clues need examination. The tidy chronology produced by an editor may be a reconstruction rather than something directly visible on the sheet.

Comparing versions helps. A phrase absent from one draft may return in another, perhaps serving a different purpose. What looks like a final rejection on a single page can become one stage in a longer process. Publication does not always end that process either; some writers revise later editions.

These limitations do not make drafts useless. They change the claims we can responsibly make. A draft can support a precise account of textual change even when the writer's private reason remains unknown. Distinguishing those questions allows the physical evidence to contribute without being asked to reveal an inaccessible inner life.

For a reader, the pleasure of drafts may lie partly in that open space. The finished work becomes less inevitable: another sentence was possible, another order tried. We can recognise the decisions visible in the record while leaving room for the ones it does not preserve. A marked page can tell us much without becoming a transparent window into its maker's mind.

questions.prompt: What does a cancelled sentence establish by itself?
options: The writer’s exact private motive
The date of every later revision
That those words were present and then rejected or displaced
That the writer abandoned the entire work
questions.explanation: It establishes a textual occurrence/change. Motive, full chronology and total abandonment need additional evidence.

questions.prompt: Why does the author question a tidy revision chronology?
options: Different inks prove a complete psychological history
It may be an editorial reconstruction from incomplete clues
Draft pages can never be compared
Every arrow records an exact date
questions.explanation: Marks may not establish timing; an editor reconstructs. Arrows/inks are limited clues and comparison is useful.

questions.prompt: What can comparison of versions reveal?
options: Every crossed-out phrase is permanently forbidden
A phrase apparently rejected may return for a new purpose
Only the published version contains language
Publication always prevents further revision
questions.explanation: The passage explicitly describes return/reuse and later-edition revision. The universal alternatives contradict it.

questions.prompt: Which claim best represents the author’s position?
options: Drafts provide no evidence worth studying
A finished work could never have taken another form
Drafts reveal textual decisions while leaving some motives inaccessible
Every visible mark directly expresses a complete thought
questions.explanation: The conclusion values visible decisions with limits on motive. It rejects uselessness, transparency and inevitability.
